vignette:
Kian, a 46-year-old software engineer, had always prided himself on his calm demeanour and logical approach, qualities that had served him well both in his military service and his civilian career. However, the last year had seen a steady erosion of that stability, tracing back to the day a familiar scent had caught him off guard. He had been a young soldier, barely out of his teens, when his reconnaissance unit was ambushed. The memory, though often fragmented, was always accompanied by the acrid smell of burning diesel and gunpowder, a scent that still made his stomach clench. He recalled the searing pain as shrapnel tore through his uniform, leaving him exposed and vulnerable, and the distant, then rapidly approaching, whine of enemy motorcycles – a sound that had meant certain death.

Now, years later, even a faint whiff of exhaust fumes or the unexpected roar of a motorcycle passing his home could instantly plunge Kian back into that moment. These triggers, once subtle, had become potent conduits to the past. He would find himself suddenly hearing the frantic shouts and the distinct crunch of boots on dry earth in his head, an auditory recall that made the memory feel terrifyingly real. As a result, his memories of the frightening event were no longer just recollections; they were like a film that played over and over in his mind, vivid and relentless. This constant replay meant Kian found it increasingly difficult to put the frightening event into words, the sheer sensory overload making verbalisation impossible. The pervasive nature of these memories, coupled with the suddenness of the triggers, had instilled in Kian an almost constant state of hypervigilance. He felt on guard even inside his own home, scrutinising every shadow, every unfamiliar sound. This heightened sense of threat meant that whenever the memories surged, Kian was convinced danger was imminent, driving him to seek safety. Consequently, he had developed a range of maladaptive strategies to cope. He stopped watching TV programmes or films that depicted any kind of combat or violence, fearing they might evoke more memories.

What started as a cautious avoidance of media soon extended to his daily life. He began to avoid going out, especially to unfamiliar places where he couldn't assess the danger, feeling threatened by strangers approaching him even in ordinary situations. The more Kian retreated, the more entrenched his fear became. His avoidance behaviours, like skipping his usual evening walks or declining invitations, meant he was no longer encountering the world in a way that might challenge his perception of threat. This cycle of avoidance, while offering temporary relief, paradoxically strengthened his belief that the world was a dangerous place, reinforcing his constant state of alert. This pervasive sense of threat made him acutely sensitive to any potential external cues, so even a distant motorcycle sound, which he might once have ignored, now immediately registered as a potent trigger. Moreover, by avoiding media or situations that might remind him of the event, he inadvertently prevented himself from processing the memories, leaving them raw and prone to replay. This persistent feeling of threat, in turn, made his intrusive memories even more vivid and frequent. The more threatened he felt, the more his mind replayed the "film" of the ambush, further solidifying his conviction that he needed to remain vigilant.

His wife, Mei, noticed the changes. Kian, a man who once enjoyed tinkering with his car and working out, now avoided exercise, fearing the elevated heart rate might mimic the physiological sensations of fear, or that being naked in the locker room might trigger his deep-seated feeling of vulnerability. His once vibrant social life had dwindled to almost nothing. He found it harder to focus at work; the constant internal vigilance pulled his attention away from complex coding tasks. The fear of external triggers, like the sound of a motorcycle, meant he started taking longer routes to work, adding significant stress to his commute and leading to missed deadlines. His avoidance behaviours, while offering temporary relief, also inadvertently sharpened his sensitivity to the very things he was trying to avoid. By staying indoors, the rare motorcycle passing by, or the smell of exhaust from a neighbour's car, became even more jarring and potent as triggers, as he had less context for them in his increasingly limited world. The maladaptive strategies he employed, while seemingly protective, had become self-perpetuating, intensifying his threat perception and making his memories feel inescapable. He had come to believe that if he ever relaxed his guard, something terrible would happen again.

Kian eventually sought help, exhausted by the relentless internal battle. He walked into the clinic, his shoulders hunched, his eyes darting around the waiting room, still feeling on guard. He was desperate for a way out of the tightening loop of fear, memory, and avoidance that had imprisoned him, but what frightened him most was the possibility that he might never truly feel safe again.
